title: Deterministic polynomial-time equivalence testing for d-DNNFs
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given two d-DNNF circuits \(C,D\), returns yes exactly when
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_C(a)=f_D(a),\]
where \(X\) is the union of the variables appearing in the two inputs?

The algorithm must work for all promised pairs, without any requirement that their internal decompositions or variable trees agree. It must give the exact yes/no answer in worst-case time polynomial in their total binary encoding length. The two circuits are supplied explicitly; no truth table, equivalence certificate, common compiled representation or source formula is supplied.
why: Equivalence testing checks whether two compiled representations express the same Boolean knowledge despite different decompositions. A deterministic polynomial-time test would support exact comparison and verification of representation changes without a probabilistic failure event. The gap between known randomized testing and the deterministic target also links this concrete compilation task to broader derandomization questions.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is an effective logical operation on a compiled representation: equivalence testing or negation.

sentences: The problem asks whether two explicit d-DNNF circuits can be tested for exact Boolean equivalence in deterministic polynomial time.
Decomposability requires disjoint variable sets at conjunctions, while determinism requires mutually exclusive inputs at disjunctions.
The circuits may use unrelated internal decompositions and need not share a variable tree.
Randomized polynomial-time equivalence testing is known, but its possibility of error does not satisfy this target.
A resolution would clarify the cost of comparing and verifying succinct compiled Boolean representations.

definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.

Equivalence concerns the same assignment in the two circuits; it does not allow renaming variables separately to obtain isomorphism. The inputs may have different numbers of gates and may mention different subsets of \(X\). Logical nonequivalence means that at least one assignment makes their outputs differ. Equal numbers of satisfying assignments do not by themselves establish equivalence. The only required output is the decision bit; construction of a distinguishing assignment is not an additional task.

For comparison with the known randomized result, a one-sided randomized equivalence test can always accept equivalent circuits while rejecting each nonequivalent pair with probability at least \(2/3\), in polynomial time using independent random bits. The target here removes randomness entirely. A probabilistic test, even with arbitrarily small failure probability, does not meet its guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the deterministic polynomial-time existence claim in the stated promise model. A positive answer must give one uniform algorithm, prove exact equivalence decisions on all promised pairs, and establish a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm; it need not produce a single pair that defeats every algorithm. A randomized algorithm, a procedure requiring a common variable tree, or a hardness result for arbitrary DNNFs without determinism does not by itself settle this problem. Neither does hardness of verifying a proposed conjunction of two circuits, which is a different input-output relation.

context_blocks.text: The 2026 source explicitly leaves equivalence across different variable trees open even for structured representations. This card retains the broader general d-DNNF question, independently stated in the knowledge-compilation map; it does not attribute that broader formulation solely to the structured-circuit paper.

Darwiche and Huang give a one-sided randomized polynomial-time equivalence test for general d-DNNFs. Their analysis includes a polynomial bound on the bit length of arithmetic values; the algorithmic claim is stronger than merely bounding the number of unit-cost arithmetic operations.

The knowledge-compilation map distinguishes exact model counting, equivalence and entailment. Efficient counting does not automatically decide whether two represented sets of assignments coincide, and a common variable order or compatible structured decomposition is an additional restriction.

The 2026 paper establishes efficiently checkable restricted restructuring steps while leaving the one-shot comparison across arbitrary trees open. Its hardness discussion for checking a conjunction relation concerns three representations and does not establish hardness of the two-circuit equivalence problem.
